caption:
What is Nan Madol? A city of 92 artificial islands off Pohnpei, in the Federated States of Micronesia.

The site core covers about 1.5 by 0.5 kilometres: stone and coral fill platforms bordered by tidal canals. The name means "within the intervals" — a reference to those canals. It was the capital of the Saudeleur dynasty until about 1628.

Carbon dating puts the start of megalithic construction around AD 1180, using large basalt stones taken from a volcanic plug on the opposite side of Pohnpei. Human activity on the site goes back to the first or second century AD.

There is no fresh water and no food at Nan Madol. Under the Saudeleurs, Pohnpeians brought both by boat. The city also worked as a control device: rival chiefs were made to live there, where they could be watched, rather than in their home districts.

Divers went looking for more. In 1978–79 Arthur Saxe reported tall coral-covered pillars offshore. A University of Oregon team in 1988–89 raised one, dissected it and found it was entirely coral — not a positioned stone column. A 2013 sonar and ROV survey found no man-made underwater pillars at all, and concluded the nearby blue hole is a natural sinkhole.

Still open: exactly why the site was abandoned. After Isokelekel overthrew the Saudeleurs, the new rulers had to grow their own food and gather their own water — that may have driven them out. A sharp population decline is another explanation.

Claims that Nan Madol belongs to a lost continent of Mu, or is far older than dated, are pseudoscience. Pacific archaeologists call such claims insulting to the Pohnpeian ancestors who built it.

Images: engraving of Nanmatal, 1883; Élisée Reclus, basalt walls at Metalanim; a 1935 book photograph; Scot Nelson, c. 1999; NOAA.
